files.lesson.md:
---
order: 2
unit: trail
title: Who can see this?
summary: "The same photo reaches different people depending on where it goes: a message to one friend, a group chat, a private account or a public post. Settings change the audience, but anyone who sees something can screenshot or forward it, so the real audience can be bigger than the one you chose. Before sharing, picture who could end up seeing it."
language: science
shape: 5e
hook: "Lena takes a photo of her art project. She could send it to her mum, to the class group chat, or post it for anyone. Who sees it each time, and who could see it later?"
---
Lena and everyone else here are made up. You do not need to say what apps you use.

## Engage: how far can it go?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to a guess: a private group feels closed, but anyone in it can pass things on."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Lena posts a photo to a private group of 12 friends. What is the most people who could end up seeing it?"
  options: ["More than 12: anyone in the group can screenshot or forward it", "Exactly 12: the group is private", "Only Lena: it is her photo"]
  actual: "More than 12. The setting chose 12 people, and each of them can screenshot or forward it to others."
```

## Explore: pick the audience

```step
stage: run
insight: "Matching each way of sharing to its audience shows that the place you share decides who sees it first."
check:
  type: match
  q: "Match each way Lena shares the photo to who sees it first."
  pairs:
    - ["A message to her mum", "One person"]
    - ["The class group chat", "Everyone in the class group"]
    - ["A private account with approved followers", "People Lena has approved"]
    - ["A public post", "Anyone online, including strangers"]
```

Was your guess right? The place you share decides who sees it **first**. After that, anyone who saw it can pass it on. The real audience can grow.

## Explain: the audience you chose, and the one you might get

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Naming two audiences, chosen and possible. The planted mistake is treating private as private for ever."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#theo"
      text: "Theo shares something he thinks is safe. Click the line where his thinking first goes wrong."
      answer: 2
      fault: logic
      misconception: private-means-private
      explain: "Line 2: Theo thinks a private group means nobody else will ever see it. Anyone in the group can screenshot or forward it."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Lena wants to share her art with her grandparents only. Which is the best choice?"
      options: ["Send it to them in a message", "Post it publicly and tell them to look", "Put it in the class group chat and ask them to join", "Make it her profile picture"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Anyone could see it, not just her grandparents.", "Her whole class would see it too.", "A profile picture is seen by everyone who sees her account."]
      explain: "A direct message reaches the smallest audience. Choose the smallest audience that does the job."
```

Every post has two audiences:

- **The audience you chose:** the person, group or followers you sent it to.
- **The audience you might get:** anyone they show, screenshot or forward it to.

Choose the **smallest audience that does the job**, and picture the second audience before you share. Settings help with the first audience: a private account, approved followers, asking before you are tagged. Nothing controls the second audience except the people in the first one, so you can help others too, by not passing on what was not meant for you.

### Theo's mistake

### Grandparents only

## Elaborate: settings that change the audience

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Years 7 and 8: account settings decide the first audience, and they often start open."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#settings", height: 560 }
hint: ["Read what each setting does before you change it.", "Meeting reminders are why Ava joined the app: keep those."]
check: { type: board, text: "Ava's settings in a made-up club app came open. Make her account as private as it can be while she still hears about meetings.", when: "s = 4 and f = 1", explain: "Profile members only, location off, ask before tags, ads off, reminders on. Settings often start open, so it is worth checking them." }
```

This is the same made-up club app as in How computers work › [Your digital footprint](../../../systems/cyber/footprint/), which goes further.

## Evaluate: a private think

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I can say who would see something first, and who could end up seeing it." }
```

**A private think** (just for you): next time you share a photo, who is the smallest audience that does the job?

```teacher
summary: "Students match ways of sharing a photo to who sees it first, find the
  mistake in treating a private group as private for ever, and learn to choose
  the smallest audience that does the job while picturing who could end up
  seeing it. Typical width (Years 7 and 8): set a made-up account's privacy
  settings on the club app board."
time: 35
timing: Engage and Explore 8 min · Explain 10 min · Elaborate 10 min · Evaluate 7 min
goals:
  - I can say who sees something first when I share it.
  - I can explain why the audience can grow after I share.
  - I can choose the smallest audience that does the job.
struggle: Students trust settings completely. The setting chooses the first
  audience; the people in it choose the second.
before: >
  **⚑ Wellbeing review:** this course is a draft. Share this lesson and these
  notes with the school's wellbeing lead before teaching, and agree the support
  pathway and any local wording.


  **If a student discloses something:** follow the school's child-protection
  procedure. Listen, don't probe, don't promise to keep it secret, and pass it
  on as the procedure says. Thank them and steer the class back to Lena and
  Theo.


  **Ground rules:** Lena, Theo, Ava and the club app are made up. Don't ask
  students which apps they use, whether their accounts are public or what has
  been shared about them. The closing think is private.


  The one idea: two audiences, the one you chose and the one you might get. No
  age rules for accounts are stated; for current rules point to the eSafety
  Commissioner (esafety.gov.au).


  Years 5 and 6: give the link with `?width=minimum` (the settings board is for
  Years 7 and 8). The board is the `cyber` widget's settings set from How
  computers work › Your digital footprint.
running:
  - "Engage: ask what 'private' means to them before revealing the answer."
  - "Explore: ask which way of sharing has the biggest first audience."
  - "Explain: draw two circles on the board, chosen audience inside, possible
    audience outside."
  - "Elaborate (Years 7 and 8): ask why the app starts with settings open."
  - "Evaluate: a quiet minute; collect nothing."
stuck:
  - see: A student says a private account keeps everything safe.
    ask: What can someone in the group do with their phone?
    fix: They can screenshot or forward. Settings choose the first audience only.
  - see: A student turns meeting reminders off on the board too.
    ask: Why did Ava join the app?
    fix: Keep what she needs; make the rest private.
  - see: A student mentions something shared about them or a classmate.
    ask: (Don't probe.) Thank them, and bring it back to Theo.
    fix: Follow up privately, and through the wellbeing team or child-protection
      procedure if needed.
stretch: Think of a time a bigger audience is the right choice (a school art
  show page, a fundraiser). What would you check first?
support: Draw the two circles on a card. Before sharing, name who is in the
  inner circle.
leads: >
  Next: pause before you post. Group chats move fast, and screenshots travel.


  Links: How computers work › Your digital footprint (the same settings board,
  with more on what apps collect).
exit:
  q: Why can a photo in a private group reach people outside it?
  a: Anyone in the group can screenshot or forward it.
explain: >
  Every post has two audiences: **the one you chose** (the person, group or
  followers you sent it to) and **the one you might get** (anyone they show or
  forward it to).


  Choose the **smallest audience that does the job**. Settings help with the
  first audience; they cannot stop a screenshot.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: "Theo's cartoon was forwarded by a friend. Who is responsible for it reaching
      the bigger group: Theo, the friend who forwarded it, or the cousin who
      shared it again?"
    prompts:
      - What could each person have done differently?
      - Does forwarding something make it partly yours?
    notes: Everyone in the chain made a choice. The poster can pause; each viewer
      can choose not to pass it on. Keep it about Theo's made-up group.
  activities:
    - at: run
      kind: activity
      title: Two circles
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Draw two circles, one inside the other. In the inner one, write who Lena
        chose. In the outer one, write who could see it later. Do it for the
        private group and for the message to her mum.
      notes: The outer circle is smallest for a message to one trusted person, but
        never zero.
    - at: investigate
      kind: discussion
      title: What could the friend do?
      minutes: 3
      do: >
        Theo's friend sees the cartoon. What are her choices? Which one stops it
        going further?
      notes: Not forwarding, and telling Theo it might hurt the teacher. Bystanders
        have power too.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Smallest audience
      type: question
      q: Lena wants feedback on her art from her art teacher only. Which is best?
      options:
        - Send it through the school's own system to the teacher
        - Post it publicly
        - Put it in the class group chat
      answer: 0
      explain: The school's own system reaches the one person who needs it.
```
